The paper develops a kernel sum-of-squares framework for adaptive conformal prediction, introducing a dual optimization formulation for scalability, a new HSIC-based hyperparameter tuning strategy, and theoretical guarantees supported by empirical evaluation. The paper is clearly written, the methodology is well-motivated, and the combination of theory, optimization, and empirical evaluation makes for a solid and timely contribution. The additional experiments on real-world datasets strengthen the empirical case and show the method’s potential across different settings.

For the camera-ready version, the authors should report coverage metrics alongside band width for all datasets to make the empirical results more transparent. They should expand the limitations section, especially discussing scalability beyond a few thousand samples, robustness to outliers under the 100% coverage constraint, and performance under asymmetric noise. Clarifying cases where the method does not outperform alternatives, improving figure readability, and introducing notation earlier would further strengthen the final version.

Thank your for your explanation on 2.b) and for the new empirical results, which I find convincing. I don't have any further questions at this stage, and remain generally satisfied with the authors' response.

**[Detailed datasets analysis]**:
1. **Concrete**: het GP is the clear winner in terms of mean width. We initially stated that kSoS and hom GP are tied looking at the large standard deviations. Following your comment we performed a t-test, which confirms that there is no significant statistical difference between hom GP and kSoS (mean/sd are computed on 10 replications). However, let us insist that mean widths obtained by homGP may be highly misleading. For instance, Figure 14 in the supplemental is a perfect example of such a situation. Homoscedastic GP and kSoS have very close mean widths, but their local coverage plots highly differ: homoscedastic GP under-covers and over-covers large portions of the input space (although in average it will satisfy the target marginal coverage). We observe this behaviour for all test cases, except for Case 4 which is very close to being homoscedastic. So from a broad perspective, when targeting adaptive bands for applications with heteroscedastic noise, homoscedastic GP should not be considered.
2. **Bike**: hom GP and kSoS perform equally well. This suggests that this case is homoscedastic, and our HSIC criterion (with the permutation test) is able to detect that automatically, while CQR and het GP struggle.
3. **Bio**: as already mentioned, this dataset exhibits largely asymmetric noise, and CQR by nature is well suited in such situation. But note that even without an optimized variant of our kSoS asymmetric extension, we are able to outperform both GPs.
4. **Diabetes / MPG**: in these new experiments kSoS achieves the smallest mean width in average.
5. **California Housing**: similarly to Bike, hom GP and kSoS yield the best results due to the suspected homoscedastic nature of the noise, which is also detected with our HSIC independence test.


Overall, when looking at the different results delivered in both the main paper for analytical datasets and this discussion with 6 real-world ones, we believe that our numerical experiments ultimately show that kSoS is a competitor worth trying to build adaptive bands in a small or moderate sample size regime. In our opinion, the only dataset where we identify more work to improve kSoS is Bio, with highly asymmetric noise. With our current version we are still unable to fill the gap with CQR, but we are confident that our planned future work on deriving new upper bounds for local coverage will help.

We hope that these additional experiments and these comments will help convince that kSoS is a method worth of interest in practice, although at the moment specifically on datasets without limitations related to kernel methods in general.

**[Positioning with respect to competitors]** You insist on the fact that only four methods are compared in our paper. This is entirely true, but we would like to point out a few facts about them:
1. We know from the paper of Romano et al. (2019) that CQR was proved to be a strongly performing method, when compared to several competitors - ridge regression, random forests, neural nets, and their rescaled version. This is why we did not consider such competitors, since it would have been rather easy to outperform them, and considered instead the best performing method of Romano et al.'s paper, that is CQR with random forests.
2. To the best of our knowledge, rescaled homoscedastic and heteroscedastic GPs have never been investigated before as competitors in CP benchmarks (except a jackknife homoscedastic GP in Jaber et al. (2025), but with no comparison with traditional adaptive CP methods). Our results show that they are in fact very strong competitors, systematically outperforming CQR on the mean width criterion for medium-size sample sizes (in the order of the hundreds), except for Bio where the noise is highly asymmetric. Of course we did not investigate dozens of datasets, but in our opinion this shows that for medium-size problems, heteroscedastic GPs are definitely worth trying to reach adaptivity (we comment on homoscedastic GPs below). This also means that in our benchmarks, we evaluated kSoS against strong alternatives, instead of going through the easy road with competitors from Romano et al. (2019), which would not be suited in our data regime and consequently not hard to top.
3. You also indicate that our experimental evaluation does not convincingly support our claims. However, in our paper we never mention that our kSoS proposal will be the best performing method in all cases, which would have been very bold and dishonest. Instead, we claim that:

   a) our dual formulation and associated AGD algorithm makes it possible to scale kSoS to datasets with several hundred samples, which was not achievable with previous kSoS work for prediction bands. Three real-world datasets with $1000$ sample points are now presented in our rebuttal, and 5 synthetic ones up to $2000$ sample points in our paper to support this claim.

   b) we can achieve good adaptivity by tuning the kernel hyperparameters with HSIC. In both our supplemental and the new tables we provide in the discussion, we think that it is fair to say that in a large majority of the considered instances, kSoS achieves better adaptivity when measured by mean width. Indeed, there are only 2 datasets among 11 (Bio which is asymmetric and Concrete), where our method is not ranked first (or in first place with ties with a GP variant) but is ranked second behind different winners. No other competitor, although they generally have strong performance, achieves this robustness. We comment in more details the obtained results in the following point.

Thank you for your additional feedback, and the new comments that we address below.

**[1.a), 1.b), 2.a)]** Thank you for the suggestion, we will add the discussion from 1.a) in the paper, and details about 2.a) in the supplemental.

**[2.b) Case 4]** Concerning the computational complexity due to the independence test, it it actually highly negligible with respect to the first step where we optimize the HSIC. Indeed, we rely on the permutation test of Gretton et al. (2007): once the samples for computing the HSIC are available (this is of course the case for computing our optimum), we just randomly permute the observations (typically $1000$ times) and compute a quantile. Since computing the HSIC is very fast (in the order of milliseconds), this last step has no impact on our total running time.

**[Experiments on real-world datasets]** Thank you for acknowledging the value of the additional experiments. In our response to Reviewer ca1L (see below), we also have results on three new datasets. We would thus end up with 5 synthetic datasets where we can quantitatively explore the local coverage achieved by all methods, and 6 real-word datasets commonly used in regression problems.

**References**

Gretton, A., Fukumizu, K., Teo, C., Song, L., Schölkopf, B., & Smola, A. (2007). A kernel statistical test of independence. Advances in neural information processing systems, 20.

Thank you for your additional comments.

**[Weakness 1]** We acknowledge your suggestion, and since Reviewer ca1L commented that our numerical experiments are still weak despite the three datasets we investigated for the rebuttal, we also performed additional experiments on three usual regression datasets which are presented in the response to Reviewer ca1L below.

**[Non-convexity from <100% coverage constraint]** This is a very good point. Actually, our idea for future work is to follow the approach proposed by Braun et al. (2025), adapt it to our framework, and then study it from a numerical perspective. In a nutshell, they have a remarkable result where they provide an exact reformulation of their optimization problem (with NP hard combinatorial structure for the coverage constraints) as a difference-of-convex programming, which can be solved with **local** optimization. They also propose a convex relaxation which can be solved globally (as in our kSoS framework), but leads to larger prediction bands. We plan to see first if we can build upon their ideas to get an exact reformulation of our kSoS problem with <100% coverage and, if this is achievable, carefully study the optimization problem we would end up with.

The added limitations section is a welcome change. Scalability limits, sensitivity to outliers, and the low-dimensional, symmetric-noise assumptions called out directly. This makes the boundaries of the approach much clearer and is a solid step toward being more transparent to the readers.

However, the experimental evaluation remains weak and does not convincingly support the authors' claims. The additional tests cover only three datasets, with kSoS clearly winning just one of them. On Concrete, it ranks third, yet the rebuttal describes it as tied for second place, which is misleading given there are only four methods compared.

Moreover, the reported numbers show only prediction interval width. One of the central promises of conformal prediction is valid coverage, yet no coverage metrics are provided for real-world data. Without this evidence, the claim that kSoS maintains conformal guarantees in practice is unsubstantiated.

Clarification on concern 2, the notion of "harmful" is in the sense that optimizing over the objective (in this case, HSIC based lower bound) resulting in an adverse effect on the final target (local coverge). This is a common phenomenon in generalization theory and robust learning theory, since using infimum (supremum) as optimization target usually invoke robustness rather than better "generalization" (in this case, local converge) in expectation (compared to naive initialization). The added simulation addressed the concern only to a certain degree, a direct comparison of local coverage between naive initialization vs optimized \theta_f would clarify the situation.

In regard to real data simulation, I believe the response is satisfactory.

Therefore, I would like to raise my score to 4.

Thank you very much for your careful reading and insightful feedback. In what follows, we address each of the points you raised.

#### **Experiments on real-world datasets**

We greatly appreciate your positive assessment as well as the constructive criticism regarding the lack of experiments on real-world datasets, as was pointed out by all reviewers.
Following Reviewer bubu’s suggestion, we have performed additional numerical experiments on 3 datasets from Romano et al. 2019: concrete (dimension 8), bio (dimension 9, with 1000 training points) and bike (dimension 18, with 1000 training points). The results of kSoS versus CQR, homoscedastic and heteroscedastic GPs is given below, in terms of mean width following Romano et al. 2019 (mean $\pm$ sd):

| **Case**   | CQR                 | Het GP                  | Hom GP                 | kSoS                 |
|------------|---------------------|--------------------------|-------------------------|----------------------|
| Concrete   | $0.586 \pm 0.032$   | $\mathbf{0.508} \pm 0.052$ | $0.543 \pm 0.044$     | $0.556 \pm 0.044$    |
| Bike       | $1.114 \pm 0.062$   | $1.000 \pm 0.079$         | $\mathbf{0.809} \pm 0.024$ | $\mathbf{0.804} \pm 0.032$ |
| Bio        | $\mathbf{1.879} \pm 0.046$ | $2.21 \pm 0.100$       | $2.194 \pm 0.119$     | $2.017 \pm 0.067$         |

On the Concrete dataset, heteroscedastic GP clearly outperforms all other methods, and kSoS is in second place with homoscedastic GPs. On the contrary, for the Bike dataset, homoscedastic GP and kSoS provide much thinner bands than competitors. Finally, the Bio dataset is the only case study where CQR performs much better than other methods. This is due to the asymmetric nature of the noise. With our asymmetric extension of kSoS, we are able to build better prediction bands than both GPs, even though we do not reach the performance of CQR. All in one, kSoS is systematically among the best methods, whatever the dataset. We hope that these new results demonstrate that our method is both effective and generalizes well across diverse settings.

#### **Discussion on limitations**

Following your comment on adding a more thorough discussion on limitations (which is also shared by all reviewers), we completely agree, and propose to add a new paragraph before the conclusion. To summarize, we will mention the following limitations:
1. Kernel SoS performs well for dimensions up to 10 or 15, a limitation shared by all kernel methods without specific strategies. For high-dimensional objects with structure (time series, probability distributions, molecules, strings, graphs,….), it is however possible and straightforward to plug specifically designed kernels in our framework. On the other hand, for high-dimensional tabular data, a common strategy is to rely on additive kernels: we plan to investigate how they could be incorporated in the kernel SoS framework in future work.
2. We showed in our numerical experiments that kernel SoS can scale up to 2000 samples thanks to the dual formulation, but handling much more samples than that would be highly time consuming. This is inherently a limitation which comes more from the kernel point of view than from the dual formulation. Indeed, each objective function and gradient computation in the dual formulation involves the usual kernel regression formulas, which scale as $O(n^3$). A usual workaround is to use Nystrom-type approximations or Random Fourier Features, which could be easily integrated in our problem. We plan to study how they perform on datasets with large number of samples in future work.
3. Due to the 100% coverage constraint, kernel SoS is less robust to outliers than CQR. In such cases, a pre-processing step using another model (e.g. the initial GP model we use in our procedure) is recommended.

All in one, kSoS is systematically among the best methods, whatever the dataset. We hope that these new results demonstrate that our method not only performs well in the original synthetic examples but also generalizes well on other datasets.

In particular, we now tackle problems up to dimension 18 with 1000 training points (see our comments related to limitations below for additional discussion on some challenges you mentioned - outliers and high-dimensional problems). Finally, you also bring up covariate shift: since our method only operates at the score construction step of split CP, it can directly be generalized to the common covariate shift setting through weighted quantiles.

#### **Discussion on limitations**

We agree that readers would profit from a dedicated limitation section so that they can grasp the boundaries of our approach. We will add a new paragraph before the conclusion, where we will mention the following limitations:
1. Kernel SoS performs well for dimensions up to 10 or 15, a limitation shared by all kernel methods without specific strategies. For high-dimensional objects with structure (time series, probability distributions, molecules, strings, graphs,….), it is however possible and straightforward to plug specifically designed kernels in our framework. On the other hand, for high-dimensional tabular data, a common strategy is to rely on additive kernels: we plan to investigate how they could be incorporated in the kernel SoS framework in future work.
2. We showed in our numerical experiments that kernel SoS can scale up to 2000 samples thanks to the dual formulation, but handling much more samples than that would be highly time consuming. This is inherently a limitation which comes more from the kernel point of view than from the dual formulation. Indeed, each objective function and gradient computation in the dual formulation involves the usual kernel regression formulas, which scale as $O(n^3$). A usual workaround is to use Nystrom-type approximations or Random Fourier Features, which could be easily integrated in our problem. We plan to study how they perform on datasets with large number of samples in future work.
3. Due to the 100\% coverage constraint, kernel SoS is less robust to outliers than CQR. In such cases, a pre-processing step using another model (e.g. the initial GP model we use in our procedure) is recommended.
4. Our findings on the hyperparameter influence only hold for the symmetric noise case (for $a$, as demonstrated in the supplemental, but also for the other ones). Additional intensive benchmarks should be conducted on asymmetric datasets.

summary.value: Conformal Prediction (CP) is a popular framework for uncertainty quantification in machine learning, valued for its ability to provide valid, non-asymptotic coverage guarantees regardless of the data distribution or underlying model. However, standard CP methods do not adapt prediction intervals to individual inputs, which has motivated recent work on adaptive extensions. This paper introduces a new adaptive CP method based on kernel sum-of-squares, a technique for approximating nonnegative functions in a reproducing kernel Hilbert space. The key idea is to learn the CP score function by solving an optimization problem regularized with a kernel sum-of-squares term (eqs. 4 to 6), which enables the construction of adaptive prediction bands. The authors generalize the representer theorem from Marteau-Ferey et al. (2020) and Muzellec et al. (2022) to their CP setting (Theorem 2), and derive a dual formulation that can be efficiently optimized with gradient-based methods, making their approach scalable to large datasets. They also study the influence of each hyperparameter and propose a novel tuning practical method using the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC) to target improved marginal coverage in local regions of the test point, based on the theoretical bound in Proposition 4. Finally, they empirically evaluate their method in synthetic regression problems and compare against a few methods (Conformalized Quantile regression with random forests, and rescaled scores with Gaussian Processes) in terms of mean width, mutual information and local coverage.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
### Strengths

- The paper is very well-written, with a clear motivation that aligns well with the interests of the NeurIPS community
- The theoretical contributions and the derived methodology appear sound and well-justified
- I particularly appreciate the authors' efforts in providing an in-depth discussion of their framework, including Section 3.2, where they examine the influence and interactions of the multiple hyperparameters. This reflects their commitment to understand the method's behavior and improving its interpretability. Additionally, their analysis leads to novel theoretical results with potential relevance beyond the scope of this work. For example, the discussion on hyperparameter tuning directly motivates Proposition 4, which establishes weak conditional validity based on a lower bound involving HSIC, and could be of interest for other adaptive CP methods
- The empirical results show that the proposed CP method is promising

### Weaknesses

1) Some aspects of the theoretical coverage guarantees would benefit from further clarification:

a) The proof of Proposition 3 is missing. While this suggests that the result is a trivial extension of standard CP arguments to their adaptive setting, it would be helpful for the authors to explicitly explain why this is the case. In particular, they should clarify how the exchangeability of the learned scores is preserved, and why their approach based on a simple split conformal scheme suffices, whereas prior related works have relied on more elaborate calibration procedures [Liang, 2022; Fan et al., 2024].

b) In Proposition 4, HSIC is actually subject to a constraint to ensure that the square root expression remains defined (i.e., its argument is nonnegative). Since this constraint depends on the value of $\alpha_2$, and hence on the kernel choice, it would be useful to discuss whether this restricts the applicability or effectiveness of the theoretical bound. If I am not mistaken, this aspect is not addressed in the paper, and it raises the question of whether there exist scenarios in which the proposed methodology (based on maximizing HSIC) may be affected.


2) The experimental evaluation is promising but limited in scope:

a) Some implementation details could be clarified. For instance, the choice of kernel used in their experiments is not given, and the sensitivity of the results to this choice is not discussed. Additionally, while Figure 3 claims scalability to "thousands of training points", Figure 3 left goes up to $n=1000$, which limits the strength of this claim.

b) More importantly, the experiments are conducted only on low-dimensional (mostly $d=1$ and up to $d=5$) synthetic regression tasks with relatively small to moderate sample sizes. While the main text reports figures showing that the proposed method performs the best, the supplementary material questions this conclusion. For example, in Cases 3 and 4, the kernel SoS CP does not always outperform competing methods. In particular, in Case 3, heteroscedastic GP performs better than kernel SoS; in Case 4 (or Case 2 with larger dimensions, in light of Remark 2) where the ideal prediction intervals are constant, kernel SoS appears to struggle in capturing this, which seems a bit counterintuitive as I would expect its adaptivity to naturally account for such case. This makes me question the relevance of kernel SoS for more realistic or complex benchmarks.

questions.value:
Given my comments in "Strengths And Weaknesses", I would be glad if the authors could address the following.

**Q1.** On clarifying Proposition 3: why is the exchangeability assumption preserved when applying a standard split conformal scheme to their adaptive learned score function? How does this justify bypassing more elaborate calibration procedures used in prior work?

**Q2.** On the validity of the HSIC-based bound (Proposition 4): how does the dependence of this bound on the kernel and the parameter $\alpha_2$ influence its applicability? Are there cases where the square root constraint limits the practical use of this result?

**Q3.** What kernel function was used in the experiments, and how sensitive are the results to this choice?

**Q4.** Could the authors discuss and illustrate the relevance of their method to more realistic or complex regression tasks?

final_justification.value:
The authors have addressed my main concerns by providing additional clarifications, empirical results, and discussions. Their explanations resolved my initial misunderstandings (e.g., 1.b), while the added details and experiments (e.g., implementation details, low-dimensional benchmarks, real-world datasets) improved the overall evaluation. The proposed addition of a section on limitations and future directions also strengthens the paper's exposition. 

Overall, I find the response satisfactory, the contributions clearer, and the empirical evidence more convincing. However, while the proposed framework is promising and flexible enough to foster future improvements and extensions (e.g., the independence test introduced during the rebuttal), its practical relevance in realistic scenarios remains more questionable to me. This justifies maintaining my current score: I vote for acceptance.

summary.value: This paper addresses the lack of adaptivity problem in conformal prediction by reframing the construction of prediction intervals as a constrained learning problem in RKHS. Specifically, the authors introduce adaptivity to the score function by estimating the uncertainty measure ($\sigma^2$) through kernel sum of squares, which is a natural technique for positive function estimation. The new algorithm is termed, kernel sum of squares (kSoS). The authors derive a new representor theorem for the band prediction problem, which shows the unique solution is supported on the finite samples. Dual formulations are provided, which can be solved through accelerated gradient descent, therefore achieving significant speed up. Furthermore, by linking local coverage to HSIC, the authors provide a principled way for hyperparameter tuning (kernel bandwidth). Synthetic data simulation is provided to show the efficacy of the proposed kSOS algorithm.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
Strength
1. The paper is mostly well written and easy to follow.
2. Strong theoretical results are provided. The new representor theorem ensures that the algorithm can operate under finite dimensional case. Dual formulation achieves impressive speed up. The HSIC based hyperparameter tunning also intuitively makes sense.

Weakness:
1. (Major) The paper only have a set of synthetic data simulation and lacks real data simulation. One suggestion is to add a small set of real data simulation comparison just like [1]
[1] Romano, Yaniv, Evan Patterson, and Emmanuel Candes. "Conformalized quantile regression." Advances in neural information processing systems 32 (2019).
2. (Major) Following weakness 1, the actual merit of Prop. 4 and the hyperparameter tuning strategy is questionable. Since the HSIC is simply appearing as part of the lose lower bound for local coverage, there is no guarantee that optimizing $\theta_f$ according to HSIC will not harm the actual performance. With very limited synthetic data simulation, the claim that such a tuning scheme would work is not well supported.
3. (Minor) The choice of hyperparameters (other than tunable parameters) are discussed in Section 3.2 with claims supported in Section 4. However, with the lack of real data simulations, it would be difficult to judge the claims. (For example, b=10 is sufficiently large)
4. (Minor) Notation definitions can be improved. For example, nuclear and Frobenius norm are defined after Eq. (4), but used as early as Eq. (2). Hyperparameter a and b are not defined.

summary.value:
This paper introduces a new method for building adaptive prediction intervals using conformal prediction. 
The main idea is to learn both a mean function and a non-negative scaling function using a kernel sum-of-squares framework. 
The method produces adaptive intervals that adjust to the local uncertainty in the data and still guarantee valid coverage. 
The authors provide a solid theoretical foundation, a dual formulation that scales well, and a new tuning strategy based on HSIC to guide adaptivity.

strengths_and_weaknesses.value:
The paper's biggest strength is how well it connects ideas from different areas—conformal prediction, kernel methods, and structured low-rank learning—and turns them into something coherent. 
It doesn't just throw these tools together. Each part is motivated: kernel SoS is used to learn a non-negative function, the split CP step gives finite-sample guarantees, and HSIC is brought in to tune adaptivity. 
The method is scalable too, thanks to a dual formulation that avoids solving SDPs. 
And the hyperparameter section is thoughtful. The authors actually explain what each parameter does and how they interact.

That said, the evaluation is limited. 
All experiments are done on synthetic data. 
These examples are useful for showing how the method behaves under different types of noise, but they don’t really tell us how it handles the messiness of real-world data—things like outliers, covariate shifts, or higher-dimensional structure. Even a single real regression benchmark would have gone a long way. 
As it stands, the results mostly validate the theory, not the practical utility.

There's also no discussion of limitations, as requested.
Some of these issues are mentioned in passing (like the difficulty of local coverage), but there's no structured effort to acknowledge the boundaries of the approach. 
A short limitations section would have made the paper feel more complete and self-aware.

title.value: Scalable and adaptive prediction bands with kernel sum-of-squares

abstract.value: Conformal Prediction (CP) is a popular framework for constructing prediction bands with valid coverage in finite samples, while being free of any distributional assumption. A well-known limitation of conformal prediction is the lack of adaptivity, although several works introduced practically efficient alternate procedures. In this work, we build upon recent ideas that rely on recasting the CP problem as a statistical learning problem, directly targeting coverage and adaptivity. This statistical learning problem is based on reproducible kernel Hilbert spaces (RKHS) and kernel sum-of-squares (SoS) methods. First, we extend previous results with a general representer theorem and exhibit the dual formulation of the learning problem. Crucially, such dual formulation can be solved efficiently by accelerated gradient methods with several hundreds or thousands of samples, unlike previous strategies based on off-the-shelf semidefinite programming algorithms. Second, we introduce a new hyperparameter tuning strategy tailored specifically to target adaptivity through bounds on test-conditional coverage. This strategy, based on the Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion (HSIC), is introduced here to tune kernel lengthscales in our framework, but has broader applicability since it could be used in any CP algorithm where the score function is learned. Finally, extensive experiments are conducted to show how our method compares to related work. All figures can be reproduced with the accompanying code at https://www.gitlab.com/drti/ksos-bands.
